quote: die $10^{(10^{10})}$ te Ziffer in der Dezimalbruchent- wickelung für $\pi$ [-...-] angeben
english: To state the 10^(10^10)-th digit in the decimal expansion of pi.
topic: Notes on freeing logic and epistemology from anthropomorphic thinking, on problems whose meta-question is best settled by solving them (twin primes, digits of pi), on a philosophical theory of experimentation and meaning applied to relativity and unsolvable problems, and on the axiomatic method in physics.

triage.modern_statement: Find the decimal digit of π at position N = 10^(10^10), meaning the N-th digit after the decimal point. A finite algorithm can always do this, so it is decidable in principle and not an open theorem. The practical question is whether the computation can actually be carried out. N has about ten billion decimal digits, so neither computing every digit up to N nor extracting that single digit is feasible. In the note, Hilbert seems to use it like the Brouwer-style examples about π's digits: a problem where the best answer to the meta-question 'is it solvable?' is simply to solve it.
triage.answered_by: No one. The digit has not been computed. The largest computation so far reached 314 trillion (about 3×10^14) decimal digits, done by StorageReview (Kevin OBrien, Divyansh Jain, Brian Beeler) with y-cruncher in November 2025. That is far short of 10^(10^10). The BBP formula (Bailey, Borwein, Plouffe, 1997) can extract single base-16 or binary digits of π, but not decimal ones. Plouffe (2022) proposed a formula for the n-th decimal digit, but I found no source showing it reaches anywhere near this position. A related Brouwer/Heyting example about π's digits was settled by computation: Kanada found the string 0123456789 in π in 1997.

evidence.claim: The current record for computing π is 314 trillion digits (StorageReview, November 2025).
The 314-trillion-digit record was set by Kevin OBrien, Divyansh Jain and Brian Beeler of StorageReview using y-cruncher.
The BBP formula yields a spigot algorithm for the n-th base-16 (hexadecimal) digit of π, not decimal digits.
MathWorld says Plouffe (2022) 'proposes' a formula for decimal digits of π, while BBP covers hexadecimal and binary digits.
Plouffe's 2022 paper 'A formula for the n'th decimal digit or binary of Pi and powers of Pi'.
Brouwer and Heyting claimed it was 'impossible' to know whether 0123456789 appears in π; Kanada found it in 1997.

triage.why: This is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. It is a well-known type of example from the intuitionism and decidability debate. No one is working on this particular digit as a research problem, and sources put it far beyond any computation done so far. Related work on record π computations and digit-extraction formulas is still going on. I chose 'open_and_known' because the digit is still unknown. 'not_research' would also be defensible, since it is a finite computation that is decidable in principle.
